records.name: France
records.current_summary:
France is very safe for a transgender visitor, with risk concentrated on two specific situations. If you are arrested for any reason, including a protest or minor offence, a trans woman is likely to be placed in a men's prison on the basis of her legal gender — a systemic practice documented with foreign trans women (Argentine, Ecuadorian) subjected to genital-exam "verification," isolation and abuse. France's own detention watchdog says trans detainees "suffer the most," and a 2025 case (Louna, held in a men's prison in isolation) drew parliamentary censure.

At the border, trans women — especially racialised or Latin-American travellers — have been humiliated by French border police (the documented Giovanna case at Paris CDG), and the airport waiting-zones draw repeated discrimination criticism.

Offsetting this: there is no restriction on bathroom use, and the social norm leans trans-inclusive (a Lyon hostel in 2024 sanctioned a guest who complained about a trans person in a female dorm as "transphobic"). Anti-discrimination and hate-crime law cover gender identity. The risk is harassment-level in day-to-day tourism, with the serious-but-rare arrest/placement axis being the main caveat.
records.current_outOfScope: Urban crime (pickpocketing, theft) in Paris and Marseille, and the general risk of civil unrest/protests, affect all travellers.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): placement of trans women in French prisons follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, creating a legal grey area — prisons improvise with special units or isolation, restricting contact with other inmates; accounts describe assault vulnerability and suicide risk. No statutory rule governs placement, so treatment varies by facility.

CGLPL (national custodial-inspection authority) opinion of 25 May 2021: reviewing roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 plus ministry and association input, finds serious, persistent violations — placement by birth sex, isolation, strip-search exposure — and notes no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite France's 2016 legal gender-recognition reform; issues binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

APT interview with France's national preventive mechanism: explains why a new opinion was issued — the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, gender-recognition law and terminology changed, and it extends coverage to intersex and non-binary detainees; cites structural problems (isolation of vulnerable people, suicide prevention) built on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

20 Minutes (4 Feb 2025): Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October — confirms that as of 2025 trans detainees are still placed in facilities matching birth sex, with isolation used as the management response.

French National Assembly oral question no. 219 (17th legislature): a deputy formally questions the Keeper of the Seals on trans inmate Louna's incarceration, arguing her case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees — official parliamentary scrutiny keeping the placement issue politically live.

StreetPress first-person account (7 Mar 2017): trans woman Giovanna Rincon describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, publicly questioned in front of other travellers — visitor-facing evidence of identity-document friction at French entry points for trans travelers.

Women's Forum Australia (Aug 2024): reports a Lyon hostel incident in which an Australian guest who objected to a man in the female dormitory bathroom was threatened with 'transphobia' by the manager — a traveller-facing dispute over sex-segregated accommodation in France, contested framing notwithstanding.

Défenseur des droits (national rights ombudsman) new framework decision on trans rights: confirms persistent fundamental-rights violations from case files and association testimony, and cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey — 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination — with official guidance for service providers.

CNN (29 May 2013): report on France's first same-sex wedding, performed days after the marriage-equality law took effect — dates the legal equality baseline relevant to partner travel and marriage recognition for visitors.

records.name: Poland
records.current_summary:
Poland is broadly workable with two genuinely traveler-relevant weaknesses and a low-but-improving social baseline. In detention, Poland has documented severe failures involving foreign trans people directly: a Vietnamese trans woman was held in a male immigration-detention center with her hormone-therapy needs ignored, and the European Court of Human Rights found Poland violated a trans prisoner's rights by denying her HRT (2024). There is no specialized trans prison section analogous to Italy's Rebibbia.

Socially, the climate was deeply hostile under the previous Law and Justice government ("LGBT-free zones") and is improving under the Tusk coalition (a hate-speech reform draft in March 2025; ceased investigating foreign same-sex marriages), but a low baseline persists — Pride marches have been violently attacked (Białystok 2019), online anti-LGBT harassment is documented (Amnesty 2025), and rural areas draw harassment warnings. Legal gender recognition is court-based and medically gatekept, with no self-ID.

Bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute. Major cities are calmer than rural areas.
records.current_localsOnly: The court-based, medically gatekept LGR regime is resident-facing; the ECtHR HRT-denial ruling concerned a resident prisoner.
records.current_outOfScope: Passport theft, unofficial-taxis overcharging, and general urban crime affect all travellers.

sources.claim: Association for Legal Intervention news (13 Mar 2024): a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after NGO intervention the Border Guard commander ordered her release. Her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused medication supply; the case also documented her prior violence and sexual-assault history. Evidence Polish detention practice can endanger trans detainees' health until challenged.

TGEU (16 Jul 2024): on 11 July the ECtHR found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (and rejected Article 3) by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy; damages of EUR 8,000 ordered. Directly relevant precedent: trans prisoners in Poland can litigate medication denial and win.

Amnesty International report 'A Thousand Cuts' (2025): documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, including LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and X's policy reversals (misgendering/deadnaming rule removed Apr 2023, reinstated 2024). Online abuse climate, not visitor law.

HRW World Report 2025 (Poland, events of 2024): LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government was 'slow and insufficient'; in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in a 'illegal vacuum' violating their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Jan-Dec 2024): Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; March draft Penal Code amendment raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech/violence, passed Government Legislation Centre in May but approval was postponed; a second bill followed in late October; Prosecutor General set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Global Affairs Canada travel advisory for Poland: lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status; links generic LGBTQ2+ travel guidance; visa-free for tourists up to 90 days. Generic advisory, limited Poland-specific finding.

Przeglad Sejmowy 2024/5, Podgorska-Rykala & Kepa: scholarly legal analysis of Poland's administrative regime for transgender persons under the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act; asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status. Evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice in Poland.

HRW news release (18 Mar 2007): the then government proposed fast-track legislation 'punishing anyone who promotes homosexuality' in schools - dismissal, fines or prison for teachers/students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with deputy minister Orzechowski announcing teachers who reveal homosexuality would be fired; HRW wrote to PM Kaczynski. Historical precedent for state-led school censorship.

records.name: Hungary
records.current_summary:
Hungary is in a fast-improving post-Orbán transition. The most acute traveler-facing risk — the 2025 Pride ban with facial-recognition identification of attendees — has stopped: the 2026 Budapest Pride was held freely. Péter Magyar's Tisza party won a supermajority in April 2026, ending 16 years of Orbán rule, and the EU's top court has ruled that Hungary's 2021 "child protection" law breaches EU values (handing the new government a repeal mandate).

However, the Orbán-era laws remain on the books: a total ban on domestic legal gender recognition (2020), the "child protection" content law, and a constitutional amendment banning LGBTQ public events. The structural weakness that has not changed with the election is detention: a German court in 2025 blocked the extradition of a non-binary person to Hungary because of prison conditions and the person's identity, and watchdogs report transphobia in prisons with a "culture of silence."

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific entry friction. Social hostility lingers outside Budapest, but the state-led demonization that characterised the Orbán years has ended.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2020 total ban on domestic legal gender recognition is resident-facing; the prison "culture of silence" affects resident detainees.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (June 2026) covers LGBTQ rights in Hungary after the election - 'we are very hopeful that changes will be made'.

AP (Jun 2026): 'Hungary holds its first Budapest Pride in the post-Orbán era' — tens of thousands march in the 31st Budapest Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of his era's anti-LGBT laws.

The Dissident analysis (April 2026) by Alejandra Caraballo: what Hungary's election (Tisza's 138 seats, ending Orbán's rule) actually means for LGBTQ people - a return to democratic baseline, not liberation. Details the 'constitutional architecture of erasure': the May 2020 total ban on legal gender recognition (redefining 'nem' as immutable biological sex), forcing trans Hungarians to carry mismatched documents.

Wikipedia country overview (live): legal gender change has been de facto impossible since 2018 and explicitly illegal since 2020; same-sex activity legal since 1961. The page carries the current legal-status table used to check the record's gender-recognition claims.

BBC News (April 2026): the European Court of Justice ruled Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws — including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law — breached EU rules on several levels, significantly finding a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty (an unprecedented finding against founding values). The ruling came nine days after Hungarians voted in the election that ended Fidesz rule.

niHaplus (17 April 2026): after Fidesz lost power in the 12 April 2026 election ending 16 years of Orbán rule, Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named restoration of the right to assembly as 'the most urgent issue' and said anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar raises questions about the pace of change.

Hungarian Helsinki Committee / Háttér Society national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, part of the EU-funded 'Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU' project - the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate.

HRW World Report 2025 (Hungary): LGBT people continue to face discrimination and demonization; a 2020 law bans legal gender change for transgender and intersex people, and in September 2024 the CJEU Advocate General called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries.

ECJ judgment C-247/23 Deldits (13 March 2025), on reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case: Article 16 GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Art 5(1)(d) — the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records.

BuzzFeed News (April 2020, Patrick Strudwick): while ruling by emergency decree during COVID, Orbán's government pushed a bill barring passports and ID cards from reflecting a person's acquired gender — even for those already legally recognized. This is the decree-level rollback that made legal gender recognition explicitly illegal in 2020.

freshness_all.fact: 2020 legal-gender-change ban stands (explicitly illegal); 2021 'child protection' law in force; NEW: March 2025 law bans organising/participating in Pride — Budapest Pride permit denied 3 June 2025

records.name: Czechia
records.current_summary:
Czechia is broadly workable with an improving trajectory and a major welcoming tourist hub (Prague), offset by unprepared detention systems and elevated baseline social hostility. Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery — the Constitutional Court struck that requirement in 2024 and the Health Ministry implemented reform in 2025 — but it still requires a medical diagnosis and 6–12 months' observation (improving, not self-ID).

If detained, the system is unprepared: the Supreme Court in November 2025 demanded prison rules for trans people, and there is a documented case of police mishandling the extradition-detention of an HIV-positive trans foreigner. About half of LGBTIQ people report being targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years, and the far-right SPD uses "deviant" rhetoric; Prague and larger cities are welcoming, but harassment is more likely in rural areas or late at night.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.
records.current_localsOnly: The LGR reform (diagnosis + observation, no surgery) is a resident-facing process; the Supreme Court's demand for prison rules concerns resident detainees.
records.current_outOfScope: Pickpocketing and fake-plainclothes-police scams in Prague affect all tourists.

sources.claim: Czech Constitutional Court, judgment PL. US 52/23 (24 Apr 2024), official legal summary: the Court struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change — sex change conditional on disabling reproductive function (sterilisation) held unconstitutional; landmark end of compulsory sterilisation for legal gender recognition in Czechia.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2025) covers Czechia dropping the surgery requirement for legal gender change.

Česká justice (20 Mar 2023, Czech): administrative courts clashed over immigration police handling of detained trans foreigner — the Supreme Administrative Court (Baxa panel) rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward an HIV-positive trans man in transition, and ruled authorities must first assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement. Visitor-relevant: detention-placement safeguards exist at supreme-court level but practice is inconsistent.

Česká justice (18 Nov 2025, Czech): Czech prisons are unprepared for trans people and lack clear rules; the Supreme Court demands the national prison concept explicitly address needs of people in or after transition, citing the Constitutional Court ruling that no longer conditions legal gender change on surgery; the human-rights commissioner pushes a binding regulation while the Justice Ministry claims the existing framework suffices (consultation ongoing). Prison-placement risk is documented and unresolved.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): 'Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia' survey — 43% discriminated/harassed in past 5 years (over a third within 12 months), highest among trans and non-binary respondents; 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats in 5 years; politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% (2018) to 71% (2023), with 63% attributing rising intolerance to politicians. June: a group disrupted Brno Pride drag story-time with homophobic slurs; new Asylum Law includes SOGI grounds with opposite-gender interview option; marriage-equality bill cleared committees 29 June while a constitutional ban moved to second reading (SPD/ODS/KDU-ČSL/ANO ~80-90%); April: Ostrava Regional Court ordered re-issued certificates/diploma for a trans graduate; no law yet ending mandatory sterilisation as of 2023.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite for legal gender recognition, the Justice Minister publicly stated his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' and other politicians issued transphobic statements; far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists' ('give more to families, take it away from the deviants'); the government approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity (pending in Parliament), while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status; school-curriculum LGBTI content prompted organised parental opt-out campaigns.
thin: no usable finding

allaboutczech travel portal (Feb 2026): Prague and Brno rated most open for LGBTQ+ solo travellers — formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts (Vinohrady, Žižkov), hostels with concierge support/private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings; practical guidance on documents, medication carriage and venues. Direct visitor-facing safety guidance.

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report, Czech Republic: police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, 46 prosecuted, 42 sentenced (LGBTI-motivated incidents included in bias breakdown); Criminal Code amendments abandon the 'hostility model' for the discriminatory-selection model; ODIHR key observation — recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes. Baseline quantification of bias-crime enforcement.

ECHR, T.H. v. the Czech Republic (App. no. 33037/22, judgment 12 Sep 2025): the Court found a violation of Article 8 regarding Czech legal-gender-recognition conditions — the surgical/sterilisation condition for official sex change and related civil-registry treatment held incompatible with private-life rights, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe as third-party interveners; the Court's reasoning frames Convention-guaranteed gender recognition through self-determination. Definitive international-law datapoint for Czech LGR posture.

Deník/ČTK (22 Jun 2018, Czech): the caretaker government backed a same-sex marriage bill introduced by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs (ANO, Pirates, KSČM, ČSSD, TOP 09, STAN) to replace registered partnerships; the Jsme fér campaign welcomed it. Dated marker of the marriage-equality legislative trail still running (per ILGA-2024, bill passed committees June 2023).

freshness_all.fact: Surgery/sterilisation requirement for legal gender change was invalidated per the cited 2024 Constitutional Court judgment; ILGA 2025 review and the cited court documents remain current.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Czech Republic

records.name: Serbia
records.current_summary:
Serbia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the Interior Ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, a masked attacker smashed the Pride information centre's front in 2025, Pride marches require heavy police protection, and testosterone HRT supply-chain disruptions have been documented.

Serbia is outside the Schengen area (border checks for foreign travellers), legal-gender-recognition reform has stalled (the Law on Gender Identity was not adopted), and the anti-discrimination law is weakly enforced — public institutions "make minimal effort." One mitigating factor is a Belgrade prison's trans-sensitive search policy, which lets trans women choose the search arrangement, though watchdogs flag training gaps.

Serbia has a lesbian prime minister (Ana Brnabić), but stalled legislation and police brutality make that largely symbolic rather than substantive protection. Major-tourist Belgrade is "conditionally" manageable with situational awareness.
records.current_localsOnly: The stalled Law on Gender Identity and the weakly enforced anti-discrimination law are resident-facing; the Belgrade prison search policy concerns resident detainees; the HRT supply disruptions affect residents.
records.current_outOfScope: General crime and border-corruption affect all travellers; Serbia is not a Schengen state so border checks apply to foreigners.

sources.claim: Balkan Insight (27 Feb 2024): Serbian authorities investigating allegations that police officers assaulted two LGBT people — a probe into police violence against LGBT citizens (outcome: investigation opened).
Da se zna! (2 Sep 2025): presentation of the association's 8th annual hate-crime report, 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024' — the standing civil-society incident register for the year.

APT (Association for the Prevention of Torture) Serbia country page, national-preventive-mechanism recommendations: the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela, Belgrade, shall let transgender women at intake choose a female officer for searches/body inspection rather than a male or combined search — a concrete custodial-rights finding for trans detainees.

HRW World Report 2025 (Serbia/Kosovo chapter): intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns in Serbia in 2024; state response to July-August protests (activist arrests, smear campaigns) highlighted rule-of-law weaknesses.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Serbia: trans people face testosterone supply shortages (Testosteron Depo); a publication analysed 70 instances of politicians' hate speech (April 2023-April 2024); the Pride Info Centre was attacked in January and announced closure in September after 20+ attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned; a Zoomer survey found three-quarters of trans/non-binary people fear job interviews due to anticipated discrimination.

US State Department 2018 Human Rights Report for Serbia: human-rights issues include government corruption, violence against journalists, and 'crimes including violence targeting Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Intersex (LGBTI) individuals'.

records.name: Croatia
records.current_summary:
Croatia is broadly workable with a cleaner documented traveler-axis profile than its Balkan neighbours: no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police-brutality case, or foreign-trans-detention case surfaced in research. The Dalmatian coast's international-tourism culture (Dubrovnik, Hvar, Split) is broadly open, and Zagreb has the Balkans' most established gay scene.

The framework is weaker than Western Europe's: legal gender recognition (available since 2015) is partial and not self-ID (it covers only some documents), there is no marriage equality (a 2013 constitutional ban), and an anti-gender movement is active. A 2024 prosecution of a host who refused to accommodate a gay couple shows enforcement works, and the President was formally criticised for outing a minister.

The Catholic-conservative climate is more marked outside the main tourist areas. Croatia is in the EU and Schengen, so border friction for most travellers is low.
records.current_localsOnly: The partial, non-self-ID LGR regime (since 2015, covering only some documents) is resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: General tourist-season crime and border checks for non-EU nationals affect all travellers.

sources.claim: Zagreb Pride documentation report (2018) on Croatia's implementation of CoE Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5: hate-crime legislation and under-reporting of homophobic/transphobic crimes, hate speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Croatia: a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); anti-gender disinformation escalating - a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featured speakers spreading misinformation with no LGBTI organisations invited; the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before.

Croatian legal journal (Igrec, 2026, Elektronicki zbornik radova Veleuilista u Sibeniku 20(1-2):191-206): analyses how police/customs/court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under Croatian law — built on the 2013 legislative amendment allowing gender-marker registration WITHOUT altering sex characteristics, working through the Criminal Procedure Act, Police Powers Act, Customs Act and prison-sentences law with case studies of search difficulties. Documents the post-2013 legal framework in practice.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Croatia (SOGI section): minority representatives say anti-discrimination provisions (employment, housing, education, health) are not consistently enforced; NGOs report the judiciary's uneven handling of discrimination cases and limited justice access, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations flagged as inadequate. Official-source evidence on enforcement gaps despite formal protections.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while the 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022 (final court ruling); open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events incl. Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; legal gender recognition framework. Reference backbone for the record's dated milestones.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers (legal since 1977, partnership/protection laws) — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Visitor-facing nightlife/PDA guidance.

European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023): transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds.

CroL (May 2014, Croatian): Split got an LGBT Centre (second in Croatia, first in Dalmatia) a month before the 4th Split Pride (7 June 2014), run by association Risp-et; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; mayor Ivo Baldasar attended the press conference. Documents organised community infrastructure on the coast.

CroL (Oct 2014, Croatian): presentation of LGBTIQ+ centre 'Druga Rijeka' in Rijeka — founded to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national/international organisations, backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy. Second major community centre documented.

records.name: Lithuania
records.current_summary:
Lithuania is broadly workable, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. The Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but there has been no legal framework regulating the procedure for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, the Seimas Ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly, and trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse. A "Protection of Minors" law limits dissemination of LGBT information (a 2024 Constitutional Court ruling weakened its same-sex-family provision). There is no criminalisation, and LT Pride 2024 drew 15,000.
records.current_localsOnly: The 17-year LGR deadlock and the workplace-harassment documentation are resident-facing; the "Protection of Minors" dissemination law is a resident/climate signal.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

sources.claim: LGL (Lithuanian Gay League) news (Sept 2025): the Constitutional Court refused to address Lithuania's 18-year trans rights gap - a significant setback; the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

LGL news (Aug 2025): could courts finally end 17 years of legal limbo for transgender rights? - the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the laws' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court.

LRT (Sept 2025): Lithuania's Constitutional Court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
LRT (May 2025): trans people in Lithuania detail workplace harassment - open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

LGL news (April 2024): the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly - inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania - Summary of the National Review 2024': second national review (after 2019) covering public attitudes, the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and negative public attitudes; notes the lack of a legal framework and strategic approach.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Lithuania: systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule complicated by his MEP immunity.

PinkNews (Sept 2013): Lithuania's parliament to consider five anti-gay and anti-trans bills - a ban on gender reassignment ('gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception'), a same-sex adoption ban, fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

PinkNews (July 2009): Lithuania's parliament passed a 'Section 28-style' law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors ('Law on the Protection of Minors'), overriding President Adamkus's veto 87-6; Amnesty called it 'a huge step backwards'.

records.name: Latvia
records.current_summary:
Latvia is broadly workable with no legal framework for gender recognition — trans people cannot legally change their gender marker, leaving those who've transitioned in a legal limbo. The most documented institutional failure is the European Court of Human Rights ruling Hanovs v. Latvia (2024), which found Latvia failed to prosecute a homophobic hate crime (the 2021 attack on lecturer Deniss Hanovs), violating the prohibition of inhuman treatment and the right to private life. There is no criminalisation, and bathrooms are unrestricted.

On the positive side, an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI asylum-seeker in 2025, showing some institutional capacity for protection. The documented hostility is less extreme than in Lithuania (no "degenerate"-rhetoric MP, no propaganda-style minors law, no systemic-trans-workplace-harassment study surfaced), which places Latvia marginally above its southern neighbour.
records.current_localsOnly: The absence of any LGR framework is resident-facing; the Hanovs case and asylum ruling concern residents.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

sources.claim: LSM feature (27 Jun 2025): civil unions for same-sex couples in force since 1 July 2024; transgender and nonbinary Latvians still lack targeted legal change — a trans immigrant describes how legal transition would invalidate his marriage and residency status, and coalition MPs say trans rights 'have not emerged as a major issue yet'; Latvia was the first EU country to elect an openly gay head of state (2023).

ECtHR press release, Hanovs v. Latvia (18 July 2024): the Court unanimously found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack - no criminal charges were brought despite the aggressor admitting anti-gay slurs; the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Latvia: an administrative court overturned denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker; the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Khanov hate-crime case after the ECtHR ruling; two people attacked in Daugavpils, with the Prosecutor General ordering the investigation reopened after police closed it; former MEP Mamikins' homophobic posts investigated (he fled to Russia).

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Nov 2024) of Hanovs v. Latvia: further clarification of states' positive obligations in homophobic-attack cases - states must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes, sending a message of zero tolerance; notes the troubling pattern of Eastern European states failing to protect LGBTI+ persons and to investigate effectively.

ILGA-Europe Latvia page: includes the July 2024 ECtHR judgment in Hanovs v. Latvia - the Court found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after Latvian authorities declined to prosecute a homophobic assault on a gay couple in Riga as a hate-motivated offence.

PinkNews (May 2007): Archbishop of Riga Cardinal Janis Pujats called homosexuality 'total corruption in the sexual arena' and 'an unnatural form of prostitution', demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and crowds of 40,000-50,000 to counter Pride, calling Pride a 'foreign-inspired action'.
Xinhua (June 2018): around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga - the annual event rotated among Baltic capitals; organised by Mozaika under the motto 'See Diversity! See Freedom!'.
